doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Buying a cheap guitar and winning over his parents
summary: He saves for a twenty dollar guitar, struggles to play along with records, then wows a dinner party with a friend's concertina. His mother later objects when he gets serious.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: piano. You know, and so forth. And maybe that’s what he thought, I don’t know. So anyway, I sort of got a guitar, I saved up my money doing errands and allowance and jobs and things like that, and I went to New York and got like a twenty dollar guitar, a terrible thing, I didn’t know any better, but I kept fiddling with it at home. And I was so embarrassed kind of that I was so lousy. You know I’d try to play along with records. Lionel Hampton I remember was one of the ones. “Rhythm, Rhythm” by Lionel Hampton, with Johnny Hodges and Allan Reuss was on it and Cozy Cole and Jess Stacey and everything. And I’d last about half a chorus before the muscles would give out. And so anyway, so one night, a friend of ours came over and he brought a little concertina along. And we went up to my room, and there was a dinner party, it was a party, you know about twenty, thirty people. And we went up and sequestered ourselves and worked out, I’ll never forget the songs, “Blue Skies,” and “Old Man River.” And we came down and gave them a little musicale. And my father, who was half in the bag, the cigar probably almost fell out of his mouth. And my mother was beaming with pride, “That’s my boy, you see, he taught himself all this himself.”
No, no. Not at that time.

Just instrumental, yeah. And from then on I could do no wrong. “Oh it’s wonderful. You should get a better instrument, da, da, da, da.” And they were all behind it until of course that moment when you pass beyond it’s for fun and it’s for high school or school and stuff, and you become very serious about it. And in middle class families, what was middle class then, now the whole definition is topsy turvy it seems, but that, and my mother of course being German had this German accent, and that’s when she said, you know, one day she said you know, “Ju mean ju vant to sit in vront of sose svink bands and go chink, chink, chink?” I said, “Yeah, Ma.”
